clue.text: Nasty little kids, with one who tears inside out, and takes potshots.

parts.note: someone who guts a fish tears its insides out, so is a gutter
to snipe is to shoot at someone from cover, taking potshots

explanation.surface: A grumble about horrible children, one a destructive brat, another shooting at passers-by.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves read as more descriptions of the children, but each is a cryptic way of describing a word: one who guts, and one who snipes.
explanation.definitionFit: Guttersnipes are scruffy, badly behaved street children, a disparaging term for urchins.

clue.text: Relative article, called out by lepers.

parts.note: an uncle is a family relative
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Seems to describe a family member's essay that lepers shouted aloud in the street.
explanation.walkthrough: Under the old law of Leviticus a leper had to cry 'Unclean!' to warn others off, so the definition is the word they called out.
explanation.definitionFit: Biblical lepers were required to warn people by crying out that they were ritually impure.

clue.text: One with a will, obviously, and an examination at a high point.

parts.note: a test is an examination
a tor is a rocky hilltop, a high point on moorland

explanation.surface: Someone determined, sitting an exam on a mountain top.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One with a will' looks like a determined person, but it is literally someone who has made a will. 'at' just places the pieces side by side; a tor is a rocky peak, common on English moors such as Dartmoor.
explanation.definitionFit: A testator is the legal term for a person who has made a valid will.

clue.text: The kind of treatment big shots might expect.

definitions.text: The kind of treatment big shots might expect.

parts.words: The kind of treatment big shots might expect
parts.note: a cryptic definition: important people are welcomed with a ceremonial strip of carpet laid out for them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Treatment' suggests medicine for injuries from big shots, but big shots are VIPs and the treatment is a lavish welcome.
explanation.definitionFit: Rolling out the red carpet means giving a guest special ceremonial honour, as for dignitaries.

clue.text: Not so old if one were holding it.

indicators.note: the two words hold the answer's letters running consecutively inside them

parts.note: the five letters sit consecutively across the join of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone saying they would feel younger if only they had something.
explanation.definitionFit: Something less old is more recent, the comparative of new.

clue.text: One from the pen takes a long time to get the bird.

parts.note: a pigpen holds pigs, so one from the pen is a pig
an eon is an immensely long period of time

explanation.surface: A convict needs years to be released, or to catch a bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One from the pen' suggests a prisoner from the penitentiary, but the pen is a pigsty.
explanation.definitionFit: A pigeon is a common bird of the dove family.

clue.text: What you do with decals is pure robbery!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: decals are stickers that you ... on a surface
second meaning: a hold-up at gunpoint is a robbery

explanation.surface: A complaint that the price of stickers is daylight robbery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pure robbery' reads as an exclamation about price, but it is a plain definition of a hold-up.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase works as a verb for fixing stickers in place and as a noun for an armed hold-up.

clue.text: Find the proper spot–but a stand-in might.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to move into your assigned position
second meaning: a substitute replaces someone, filling that person's role

explanation.surface: Advice to settle in your assigned position, noting a substitute could do it instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means both going to your own position and substituting for another person.

clue.text: Just a wild guess, but you can't see who fired it.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a guess made with little information

definitions.text: you can't see who fired it
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a gun discharged at night, when the shooter is invisible

explanation.surface: Someone admits their guess is wild, comparing it to an unseen sniper.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a random attempt is literally a gunshot fired where nobody can see.

clue.text: What you are if they said you did wrong.

definitions.text: What you are if they said you did wrong.

parts.words: What you are if they said you did wrong
parts.note: a cryptic definition: being charged with wrongdoing gives you this status

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a remark about being blamed; it is just describing a defendant's status.
explanation.definitionFit: A person charged with a crime or blamed for a fault holds this legal status.

clue.text: Jocular, with what goes with a wig on the old movie star.

parts.note: wigwag is a set phrase, so wag is the word that pairs with wig
Lillian Gish was a star of silent films

explanation.surface: A joke about a toupee perched on a faded screen idol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wig' suggests a hairpiece, but the phrase in mind is wigwag, a word for waving back and forth.
explanation.definitionFit: Waggish means playful and humorous, like a wag or joker.

clue.text: Dropsy, to a point made wrong.

indicators.note: made wrong means the letters are set out of their right order

parts.note: E is a compass point, east

explanation.surface: Seems to say the disease reduces some point to a mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: Dropsy is the old name for swelling caused by fluid in the tissues, now called edema.

clue.text: When you hit it in the plane, you might hit the ceiling if your seat belt isn't on!

definitions.text: When you hit it in the plane, you might hit the ceiling if your seat belt isn't on!

parts.words: When you hit it in the plane, you might hit the ceiling if your seat belt isn't on
parts.note: a cryptic definition: a sudden drop in flight throws unbelted passengers upward, and hitting the ceiling also means losing your temper

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit the ceiling' is an idiom for getting angry, but here it is meant literally, as the aircraft lurches downward.
explanation.definitionFit: An air pocket is a region of turbulence that makes an aircraft drop suddenly.

clue.text: A fool, backward in North Carolina, briefly comes to a mystical utterance with the inside information.

indicators.note: backward tells you to read the word in from right to left

parts.note: NC is the postal abbreviation for North Carolina
om is the sacred syllable chanted in Hindu and Buddhist meditation
poop is American slang for inside information, the lowdown

explanation.surface: A long tale of a fool from the Carolinas who mutters mystically while in the know.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward in' looks like a description of the fool, but 'backward' turns the word IN round to NI.
explanation.definitionFit: A nincompoop is a silly, foolish person, a simpleton.

clue.text: One seated on the bench has to pull it out to make music, but it's not from the bottom of your heart!

definitions.text: One seated on the bench has to pull it out to make music, but it's not from the bottom of your heart!

parts.words: One seated on the bench has to pull it out to make music, but it's not from the bottom of your heart
parts.note: a cryptic definition: an organist on the organ bench pulls out a knob to select a rank of pipes, and the heart is an organ whose stopping would be a different matter

explanation.walkthrough: The bench sounds like a judge's, but it is the organist's seat; the heart joke plays on organ as a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ stop is the knob on a pipe organ that brings a set of pipes into play.

clue.text: Nothing to write about which is not closed.

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing
to pen something is to write about it

explanation.surface: Remarks that there is nothing to report about an unsealed thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something open is unshut, the opposite of closed.

clue.text: Matches a mixed-up plan's outlines.

indicators.note: mixed-up tells you the letters of the preceding words are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: Seems to say a confused plan matches its own sketches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Matches' looks like the verb or the definition, but 'mixed-up' tells you to jumble it along with 'a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Schemata is the plural of schema, a diagrammatic outline of a plan.

clue.text: What's the point to the ref being like, well, with water.

parts.note: S is a compass point, south
ump, short for umpire, is a sports referee

explanation.surface: A baffled question about what the referee is like, followed by a vague mention of water.
explanation.walkthrough: Ump is the American short form of umpire, the official who referees baseball.
explanation.definitionFit: A sump is a pit or well where water collects so that it can be drained away.

clue.text: Pa's partner is on the edge, to a degree, but it might be played well.

parts.note: Ma partners Pa as mother and father
a rim is an edge
BA is a Bachelor of Arts degree

explanation.surface: Mother is nervous, close to the brink, but may yet perform well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well' reads as a verdict on the playing; the definition simply says this thing is played.
explanation.definitionFit: The marimba is a wooden percussion instrument struck with mallets, so it is played.

clue.text: A well-known movie they used to go by.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: John Ford's classic 1939 western
second meaning: a horse-drawn coach that people once travelled by

explanation.surface: Nostalgia for a famous film people used to recall it by.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of the famous John Wayne western is also the name of an old passenger coach.

clue.text: She was changed into a spider for her presumption as a weaver.

definitions.text: She was changed into a spider for her presumption as a weaver.

parts.words: She was changed into a spider for her presumption as a weaver
parts.note: a general-knowledge definition from Greek myth: the weaver who challenged the goddess Athena

explanation.walkthrough: This is straight mythology: Ovid tells how the mortal woman outwove Athena and was turned into a spider.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Arachne beat Athena at weaving and was punished by transformation, giving us the word arachnid.

clue.text: It might be a turn to have a bash on one–one from Africa.

parts.note: a U-turn, so U stands for a turn
a bang is a heavy blow, a bash
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Suggests a performer's act includes knocking someone, then mentions an African.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'turn' looks like a stage act, but it is the U of a U-turn.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ubangi are a people of central Africa, named after the river region.

clue.text: "George Gordon"–by Reagan.

parts.note: a cryptic definition: George Gordon was the poet's given name, and his surname splits as BY plus Ronald Reagan's short name

explanation.walkthrough: The quoted name is the poet's own given name; the rest jokes that his surname is 'by Ron', Reagan being known as Ron.
explanation.definitionFit: George Gordon Byron, the sixth baron, was the Romantic poet known by his title.

clue.text: Uprooted trees to plant again.

indicators.note: uprooted trees are dug up and disturbed, so the word's letters are moved about

explanation.surface: Describes trees dug up so they can be planted somewhere else.
explanation.definitionFit: To reset a plant is to set it in the ground once more, a gardener's sense.

clue.text: Hoarded by Squirrel and Moose? No, but a close relative.

indicators.note: the letters are stored away inside the phrase, as a squirrel hoards nuts

parts.note: the letters run consecutively from the end of the first word through the middle one

explanation.surface: Rocky the Flying Squirrel and Bullwinkle the Moose, the cartoon pair, seem to be stockpiling something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hoarded by' says the answer is stashed inside the cartoon pair's names. The answer is not a moose itself, the clue says, but a related horned animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The eland is a large antelope, a horned ruminant related to deer such as the moose.

clue.text: Fixes things up in concrete.

parts.note: a cryptic definition: fixing things up suggests repairing them, but here it means binding them firmly, as the powdery ingredient of concrete does

explanation.walkthrough: 'In concrete' sounds like 'definitely', but it is literal: the ingredient that sets concrete hard.
explanation.definitionFit: To cement is to bind firmly, as the lime binder does in concrete and mortar.

clue.text: One of the first things a school kid had to confront.

definitions.text: One of the first things a school kid had to confront.

parts.words: One of the first things a school kid had to confront
parts.note: a cryptic definition: 'things' suggests lessons, but it is a person standing at the front of the class

explanation.walkthrough: The clue invites thoughts of the alphabet or sums; the thing faced is the adult in charge of the classroom.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil's first encounter at school is with the instructor in charge of the class.

clue.text: Athenian dramatist whose uncertain airs went on top of Shane, also uncertain.

indicators.note: uncertain airs are unsettled, so the letters of the word are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written from the clue

indicators.note: the same instruction again, so the name Shane is jumbled too

explanation.surface: A Greek playwright's shaky tunes riding on Shane, the western hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncertain' jumbles AIRS to ARIS, TOP is kept as written, then 'also uncertain' jumbles SHANE to HANES; 'went on' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristophanes was the great comic playwright of ancient Athens, author of The Birds and The Frogs.
